summary:
Our project, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, is an interactive tool that helps people explore Mars and understand the challenges astronauts may face when traveling across its surface. We developed a 3D Mars globe and a detailed map of Jezero Crater using real NASA data and images.

Users can choose two locations and compare different routes based on distance, travel time, terrain difficulty, and estimated radiation exposure. The application also shows elevation changes, terrain warnings, and estimated resources needed for a journey.

Our project addresses the challenges of future Mars exploration by showing how technology and scientific data can help astronauts make better decisions when navigating an unfamiliar environment. We believe this is important because surviving on Mars will require more than simply reaching a destination. Astronauts must understand the terrain, consider possible risks, and carefully manage their limited resources. Our goal is to make these challenges easier to explore and understand while inspiring more people to take an interest in space exploration.

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map ; Mars Survival

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is an interactive Mars exploration and route-planning application designed to help users explore the terrain of Jezero Crater and evaluate potential walking routes for future human missions to Mars.

The application combines real planetary imagery and elevation datasets from NASA with terrain analysis, route optimization, and environmental modeling. Users can explore Mars through an interactive 3D globe, switch to a detailed 2D map of Jezero Crater, select starting and destination points, and compare different routes based on distance, travel time, terrain difficulty, elevation changes, and estimated radiation exposure.

The system uses Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on an eight-connected terrain grid to calculate four different route options:

  • Shortest Route: Minimizes total three-dimensional travel distance.
  • Fastest Route: Estimates walking time while accounting for terrain slope.
  • Lower Risk Route: Considers terrain steepness and modeled radiation exposure.
  • Science Route: Prioritizes paths that pass near designated scientific exploration targets.

The application also includes a resource calculator that estimates mission duration and consumable requirements using adjustable assumptions about walking speed, endurance, and resource consumption.

Its terrain analysis uses NASA's MOLA elevation data, high-resolution HiRISE Digital Terrain Models, and processed CTX elevation tiles. Environmental conditions such as temperature, atmospheric pressure, and dust can be explored through user-selected scenarios.

Importantly, the application distinguishes between measurements calculated from actual terrain datasets and estimates based on assumptions, making its limitations transparent.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project provides several important benefits for planetary exploration, scientific education, and future mission planning.

  • Improved route awareness: Helps users understand how terrain elevation, slope, and distance affect movement across the Martian surface.
  • Comparative route planning: Allows users to compare routes based on different objectives instead of relying on distance alone.
  • Terrain hazard awareness: Identifies steep slopes, elevation changes, and areas without valid elevation data that may affect mobility.
  • Radiation awareness: Introduces radiation exposure modeling using measurements from NASA's Curiosity rover as a reference.
  • Mission resource estimation: Demonstrates how travel time and endurance assumptions influence estimated resource requirements.
  • Scientific exploration: Helps identify potential routes near designated science targets.
  • Educational value: Makes complex planetary datasets and terrain analysis accessible through an interactive visual interface.

By combining these capabilities, the project demonstrates how scientific data and computational methods can support more informed decisions about exploring unfamiliar planetary environments.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our long-term vision is to contribute to safer, more informed, and more efficient human exploration of Mars.

As space agencies and researchers prepare for future crewed missions, understanding the Martian environment will be essential. Astronauts will need to travel across unfamiliar terrain while considering mobility constraints, environmental conditions, radiation exposure, and limited mission resources.

Our project demonstrates a potential approach to addressing these challenges through data-driven route planning and interactive terrain visualization.

The intended impact includes:

  • Supporting research and education related to human exploration of Mars.
  • Demonstrating how real planetary datasets can be transformed into practical exploration tools.
  • Encouraging safer route-selection strategies by making terrain and modeled environmental risks visible.
  • Raising awareness of the challenges associated with human survival and mobility on Mars.
  • Providing an extensible foundation for integrating additional scientific datasets and more advanced environmental models.

Although the current application is an educational and research prototype rather than certified mission software, it establishes a foundation that could be expanded with additional NASA datasets, improved radiation models, real environmental observations, and more detailed surface hazard detection.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the application using a combination of web technologies, scientific data processing tools, and computational algorithms.

Programming languages:

  • JavaScript for interactive map functionality, terrain visualization, and route-planning logic.
  • Python for scientific data processing, terrain preparation, and automated testing.
  • Ruby for the Rails application framework.
  • HTML and CSS for the user interface and responsive design.

Frameworks and development tools:

  • Ruby on Rails 7.1.6 for application structure and server functionality.
  • Node.js 20+ for JavaScript development and automated testing.
  • NumPy for numerical and scientific data processing.
  • Playwright for browser-based testing.
  • npm for dependency management and test execution.

Scientific datasets and technologies:

  • NASA MOLA MEGDR for regional Martian elevation data.
  • NASA Mars Trek Viking VIS imagery for global Mars visualization.
  • NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona HiRISE Digital Terrain Models for high-resolution local terrain analysis.
  • NASA CTX elevation datasets for additional terrain sampling.
  • Curiosity Radiation Assessment Detector measurements as a reference for radiation modeling.

Algorithms and computational methods:

  • Dijkstra's algorithm for terrain-based route optimization.
  • Three-dimensional distance calculations using horizontal distance and elevation differences.
  • Slope-based walking speed estimation.
  • Terrain horizon and sky view factor modeling for estimated radiation exposure.
  • Gaussian proximity functions for science-target-oriented route planning.

The project was developed using standard computer hardware and software development environments. No specialized space hardware was required.

5. How is your project creative?

The creative aspect of our project is the way it combines planetary science, interactive visualization, and practical survival-oriented decision-making into one application.

Instead of simply displaying a map of Mars, we transformed real Martian terrain data into an interactive exploration environment where users can investigate locations and evaluate possible journeys.

One of our key creative decisions was to provide four different route-planning objectives. A route that is shortest in distance may not be the fastest or the least risky. By presenting multiple alternatives, the application demonstrates the complexity of navigating an extraterrestrial environment.

Other creative elements include:

  • Combining a rotatable 3D Mars globe with a detailed 2D Jezero Crater exploration map.
  • Turning real elevation datasets into an interactive terrain-based navigation system.
  • Integrating terrain slope and modeled radiation exposure into route comparisons.
  • Connecting route planning with mission resource estimation.
  • Allowing users to experiment with environmental scenarios and adjustable mission assumptions.
  • Providing elevation profiles, terrain warnings, and scientific target information to explain route characteristics.

We also focused on scientific transparency. The application identifies which results come from measured terrain data and which depend on assumptions. This makes the experience more educational and scientifically responsible.

6. What factors did your team consider?

During development, we considered several scientific, technical, operational, and user-experience factors.

Scientific accuracy and data reliability: We prioritized real NASA planetary datasets and considered their spatial resolution, coverage, source metadata, and limitations. We also distinguished actual measurements from modeled estimates.

Terrain and mobility constraints: We considered elevation differences, slope, horizontal distance, three-dimensional distance, and the limitations of available terrain grids. Routes avoid invalid elevation cells and terrain exceeding the configured slope threshold.

Radiation exposure: We incorporated a radiation reference rate measured by Curiosity at Gale Crater, while recognizing that this is not a direct measurement of radiation conditions at Jezero Crater.

Environmental uncertainty: Temperature, pressure, and dust conditions are adjustable scenarios rather than live observations. This allows exploration of different conditions without presenting assumptions as verified facts.

Mission resources and endurance: We considered estimated travel duration, walking speed, endurance, and consumable requirements to demonstrate how mobility decisions can affect mission planning.

Computational efficiency: Processing large planetary datasets requires balancing terrain resolution, memory usage, and performance. We therefore used appropriately sized planning grids and processed terrain tiles.

User experience and accessibility: We designed an interface with interactive maps, clear terrain legends, coordinate readouts, route comparisons, elevation profiles, and responsive controls.

Reliability and validation: We developed automated tests for terrain calculations, data loading, route planning, map behavior, and interface functionality.

Future scalability: We considered how additional datasets, improved environmental models, and more detailed terrain information could be integrated into future versions.

Ultimately, our goal was to create a scientifically grounded, accessible, and expandable demonstration of how technology can help humans understand and prepare for the challenges of exploring Mars.

Conclusion

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map transforms real Martian scientific datasets into an interactive terrain exploration and route-planning experience. By combining planetary visualization, route optimization, terrain analysis, radiation estimation, and resource calculations, the project demonstrates how computational tools can support future extraterrestrial exploration.

Our project is not just about finding a path across Mars. It is about understanding the environment, evaluating possible challenges, and demonstrating how data-driven technology could help humanity prepare for life and exploration beyond Earth.
